title: How accurate and reliable are physical function measures in people living with obesity?
official: Psychometric Evaluation of the Reliability of Functional Outcome Measures in people with obesity (PERFORMS)
summary:
Background and study aims
Adults who are overweight or living with obesity have an increased risk of health problems, such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease, and every day physical tasks can be harder to perform. We call this ‘impaired physical function’. Adults living with obesity can have similar physical function and strength levels to a person of healthy weight who is 10-20 years older. Having other problems, like diabetes, may make physical function worse. Certain interventions, such as exercise or diet, might help to improve physical function.
There are many ways to measure physical function, including timed walking tests, balance tests, and tasks that require muscle activity (e.g., sitting and standing from a chair) repeated as many times as possible within a set time. One benefit of these tests is that they can be performed in everyday settings without expensive equipment (such as at a healthcare appointment), allowing GPs and other healthcare providers to use them.
Currently, we do not know which physical function tests work best in people who are overweight or living with obesity, who also have low muscle strength. We also do not know how having diabetes may impact physical function and strength in this population. We want to measure lots of different physical function tests, to find out which tests:
1. Give us the best understanding of physical function, when compared to more expensive, complicated tests from a research centre
2. Will give similar results if performed more than once in a short time period
3. Can be performed safely by people who are overweight or living with obesity

Who can participate?
The study will include two groups:
1. People with type 2 diabetes (T2D) who are overweight or living with obesity.
2. People without type 2 diabetes who are overweight or living with obesity.
Everyone taking part will have low muscle strength and be aged 60 years or older.

What does the study involve?
Participants will have their physical function measured twice, about 1 week apart:
1. Baseline: The physical function tests will be carried out.
2. Follow-up: The same tests will be repeated 7 ± 3 days later. There will be no treatment or intervention between the two assessments.
The tests at both timepoints will be carried out at roughly the same time of day to make the results more comparable.
Each assessment (baseline and follow-up) will be divided into two separate visits. This gives participants enough time to recover between tests, reduces the amount of testing they have to do in one day, and makes scheduling more flexible.

Physical function tests:
Handgrip strength: Participants will squeeze a hand-held device as hard as possible for five seconds, three times on each hand. The highest value reached for each hand is recorded. 
Sit to Stand Test-30: The number of chair stand repetitions completed in 30 seconds, without using the hands for assistance.  
Short Physical Performance Battery: Comprises three tasks of daily living (i.e., sit-to-stand test for five repetitions, 4-metre walk test, and a simple balance test), whilst being timed.
Six Minute Walk Test: The distance walked around two cones, placed either 10 m or 30 m apart, in 6 minutes is recorded.
Stair Climb Power Test: The time taken to walk up a flight of 8 stairs as quickly and as safely as possible is recorded, both without carrying any weight, then whilst wearing a vest that weighs 10% of the participants' body weight. 
Timed Up and Go: The time taken to stand from a chair, walk to a cone 3 meters away, turn, return to the chair and sit down again.

Additional tests: 
As well as physical function tests, participants will have their weight, waist circumference, blood pressure and heart rate measured. They will be asked to provide a blood sample, complete a treadmill exercise test, leg strength test and undergo some full body scans (DXA scan) showing the amount of fat and muscle in their body. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants will receive a clear, easy-to-understand review of their physical function, body fat and muscle balance, overall fitness, and heart health. 
Body composition assessed using dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA): This procedure uses ionising radiation to form images; this is at a very low dose and any risks are negligible. 
Treadmill exercise test: Participants will be required to wear a mask over their nose and mouth, which measures the air they breathe in and out. The face mask might feel slightly uncomfortable because it must fit tightly. Participants may also feel tired and out of breath towards the end of the test.
Blood sampling: Carries a small risk of causing inflammation, tenderness of the surrounding area and bruising. However, the likelihood of these occurring is minimal. 
Participants may also feel a little tired or out of breath toward the end of the physical function tests. 

Where is the study run from?
This trial will be conducted within the Leicester Diabetes Centre (University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust) and Diabetes Research Centre (University of Leicester) which are jointly situated at the Leicester General Hospital (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to December 2027

Who is funding the study?
Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc. (USA)

Who is the main contact?
Sam-Briggs Price, PERFORMSstudy@leicester.ac.uk
conditions: Adults, with overweight or obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes (T2D), and low muscle strength

interventions.name:
A prospective, observational psychometric study designed to evaluate the measurement properties of commonly used performance-based outcome measures (PerfOs) of physical function in adults living with overweight/obesity, with and without T2D, and low muscle strength. 

Two cohorts will be studied:

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged ≥60 years
2. Males and females
3. Low muscle strength as measured by handgrip strength (corrected for BMI):
3.1. Men: <1.00 kg/kg/m2
3.2. Women: <0.56 kg/kg/m2
4. Minimum functional capacity:
4.1. Self-reportedly able to walk one block (approximately 100 metres) independently, without the use of an assistive device
4.2. A Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) total score of ≥4 (no upper limit)
5. Willing and able to consent to participate in the trial
6. Able to understand written and spoken English

Additional cohort inclusion criteria:

Cohort 1 (diabetes):
1. Living with overweight and/or obesity, defined as a body mass index (BMI) ≥27.0 kg/m2
2. Diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (T2D) defined as a HbA1c ≤10%, and managed with either:
2.1. Diet and exercise alone, or
2.2. Diet and exercise plus 0-3 oral glucose-lowering agents: metformin, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i*), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP4i), glinides (meglitinides), and sulfonylurea. *Use of an SGLT2i for indications such as chronic kidney disease or heart failure is permitted, provided the agent is not being used as part of an intensified glycaemic management regimen.

Cohort 2 (non-diabetes):
1. Living with overweight and/or obesity, defined as a BMI ≥30.0 kg/m2, or a BMI ≥27.0-<30.0 kg/m2 with at least one of the following weight-related comorbidities or risk factors: hypertension, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome, dyslipidaemia, prevalent or previous cardiovascular disease (e.g., stable heart failure), polycystic ovary syndrome, history of gestational diabetes, taking hypertensive medication or taking lipid-lowering medication).
Exclusion criteria:
1. Living with type 1 diabetes
2. Any comorbidities that may limit function (e.g., severe polyneuropathy, severe osteoarthritis, neurodegenerative disorders, requiring devices to perform activities of daily living, etc.) in the opinion of the investigator
3. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) use within six months of screening or planned initiation during the study
4. A self-reported change of body weight >5 kg within 90 days of screening.
5. Treatment with any medication specified for the purpose of weight loss or may cause significant weight change (e.g., oral or systemic corticosteroids, thiazolidinediones,  atypical antipsychotics etc.) within 90 days of screening
o	Note: thyroid hormone replacement therapy is allowed if stable dosing ≥30 days prior to screening
6. Impaired renal function is defined as estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 ml/min/1.73m2 calculated by the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation at screening.
7. Previous bariatric surgery or planned bariatric surgery during the duration of the study.
8. Participated in any clinical research study evaluating another investigational drug, including biologics or therapy, including specific immunotherapy, within 90 days or 5 half-lives for an investigational biologic drug (whichever is longer), or at least 4 weeks for other non-biologic investigational drugs, prior to the screening visit
9. Any of the following: myocardial infarction, stroke, diagnosed heart failure or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, pacemaker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator or hospitalisation for other cardiac event within the past six months
10. Serious illness with life expectancy < 1 year or other significant illness or disability which, in the opinion of the PI or study clinician, precludes involvement
11. Blood pressure > 160/100 at screening visit (Visit 1),  unless the investigator determines on repeat evaluation that the elevation is transient, not clinically significant, and does not increase risk for participation
12. Active or untreated malignancy or in remission for less than 3 years
13. Presents any concern to the investigator that might confound the results of the study or poses an additional risk to the participant by their participation in the study

Additional cohort exclusion criteria:

Cohort 2 (non-diabetes):
1. Use of any glycaemic-lowering agent (metformin, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP4i), thiazolidinediones (TZD) and sulfonylurea) within 3 months of screening
2. Diagnosis of T2D, determined as previous diagnoses of diabetes with a HbA1c <6.5%
